# T1 Relaxation

{{< include "includes/WIP-callout.qmd" >}}

---

This chapter and the next describe two of the three basic sources of MR contrast: $T_1$ and $T_2$ relaxation. We will describe how to measure the third, proton density (*PD*), later in the notes.

## Two components of net magnetization

![The net magnetization has two components.](images/ch07/the-net-magnetization-is-summarized-by-two-compone.png){#fig-ch07-the-net-magnetization-is-summarized-by-two-compone}

The net magnetization vector can be separated into two components: its projection onto the $z$-axis, which we call the *longitudinal component* $M_z$, and its projection onto the $x$-$y$ plane, the *transverse component* $M_{xy}$.

As we saw in the previous chapter, the transverse component precesses around the $z$-axis and induces a voltage in the receive coil. The coil does not directly detect $M_z$. So what determines the longitudinal component, and how can we measure it indirectly?

The two components belong to the same net magnetization, but they change for different physical reasons. This is what makes MRI versatile: one instrument can be sensitive to different properties of the tissue.

## Parallel and anti-parallel states

![The longitudinal component:  High- and low-stability states (Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e, Fig. 3.6).](images/ch07/the-longitudinal-component-high-and-low-stability.png){#fig-ch07-the-longitudinal-component-high-and-low-stability}

A proton’s spin component along $B_0$ has two possible states: parallel and anti-parallel. At thermal equilibrium, slightly more protons occupy the lower-energy, parallel state. A loose metaphor to understand this difference is shown in @fig-ch07-the-longitudinal-component-high-and-low-stability. The image shows two bars in a gravitational field, one that is hanging low and is in a low-energy state. It will stay that way unless a strong breeze comes along to move it.

The other bar is upright in a precarious state that is higher energy and less stable—even a weak breeze might cause it to fall over, dropping into the low-energy state.

The metaphor is useful, but it has limits. Protons are not tiny bars, and the net magnetization can point in intermediate directions in the vector description, especially after RF excitation. Here, “parallel” and “anti-parallel” refer specifically to the two possible outcomes for the spin component along $B_0$.


## An RF pulse changes spins between the two states

![Energy from an RF pulse changes spins between the two stable binary states (Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e, Fig. 3.9).](images/ch07/energy-from-an-rf-pulse-changes-spins-between-the.png){#fig-ch07-energy-from-an-rf-pulse-changes-spins-between-the}

The longitudinal net magnetization is proportional to the difference between the populations of the two states. An RF pulse can alter this population difference by driving transitions between the two states. The energy required for those transitions is determined by the separation between the two energy levels.

## Spin transition and quantum energy

![Spin Transition and Quantum Energy (Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e, Fig. 3.8).](images/ch07/spin-transition-and-quantum-energy.png){#fig-ch07-spin-transition-and-quantum-energy}

For proton spins the energy separation between the parallel and anti-parallel states increases linearly with the main field, $B_0$. This separation is called the **Zeeman splitting**.

An RF field at the resonant frequency can drive transitions between the two states. In the photon picture, the energy of one RF quantum is proportional to the frequency, with Planck's constant as the constant of proportionality.

$$
\Delta E = h f_L.
$$


## The frequency depends on the $B_0$ field

![The Larmor frequency depends on the $B_0$ field: $f_L = \gamma B_0$, so the resonant frequency is 127.4 MHz at 3 T.](images/ch07/the-larmor-frequency-depends-on-b0-field-1.png){#fig-ch07-the-larmor-frequency-depends-on-b0-field-1}

Putting these two facts together, we see that a higher $B_0$ requires a higher resonant frequency, $f_L$.

The relationship between magnetic-field strength and resonant frequency is linear. This frequency is called the *Larmor frequency*, after [Joseph Larmor](resources/joseph-larmor.qmd). It is the frequency an RF pulse must have to affect protons in a particular $B_0$ field.

The Larmor frequency is

$$
f_L = \gamma B_0,
$$

where $\gamma$ is the gyromagnetic ratio (42.58 MHz/T for hydrogen). At 1.5 T we excite and receive near 64 MHz, at 3 T near 127 MHz, and at 7 T near 300 MHz—all in the radio band. Higher field strength means a larger energy gap between the two spin states, a larger equilibrium population difference, and generally a larger MR signal. This is one important reason for building higher-field scanners.

## Axonal cross section

![Water in the axonal cross-section.](images/ch07/visualization-of-the-spin-lattice-exchange-1.png){#fig-ch07-visualization-of-the-spin-lattice-exchange-1}

## Hydration layer

![Hydration layer.](images/ch07/visualization-of-the-spin-lattice-exchange-2.png){#fig-ch07-visualization-of-the-spin-lattice-exchange-2}

:::

When a spin transitions from the high-energy state (anti-parallel) to the low-energy state (parallel), it gives off some energy. The energy has to go somewhere, so it is transferred to the surrounding molecular environment—the *lattice*. This is why $T_1$ relaxation is also called *spin-lattice relaxation*.

How quickly the transfer happens depends on the tissue around the spins. This is what makes $T_1$ useful: in brain tissue, values range from a few hundred milliseconds for fat to several seconds for free water.

So how are we going to use MRI to measure tissue properties?  The build shows a cross-section through a single axon, with the individual wraps of myelin visible, and then a schematic of one layer of the myelin membrane: a lipid bilayer surrounded by water molecules.

The MR properties of water change when it interacts with a membrane surface. The water immediately in contact with the membrane—the *apparent hydration layer*—has different relaxation behavior from water farther away. A model based on quantitative $T_1$ and proton-density mapping can estimate the apparent fraction of water interacting with membrane surfaces, which we will call the apparent hydration-layer fraction (aHLF) [@mezer2013-mtv]. This is an indirect, model-based estimate; in white matter, it is expected to be higher where membrane surface area and myelin are greater.

## Example: longitudinal relaxation

![Example: longitudinal relaxation.](images/ch07/example-longitudinal-relaxation.png){#fig-ch07-example-longitudinal-relaxation}

Let's zoom out from individual spins to a beaker containing many spins. @fig-ch07-example-longitudinal-relaxation shows the net magnetization at several points. It begins at equilibrium in the $B_0$ field. A resonant RF pulse then tips it 90 degrees away from the $z$-axis, so that $M_z=0$ immediately afterward. Over time, the longitudinal component recovers toward its equilibrium value,

$$
M_z(t) = M_0\left(1 - e^{-t/T_1}\right)
$$

Note that this equation is for the 90 deg flip angle case: it assumes the longitudinal component starts at zero.  The slide asks what would happen with a 180 deg flip angle, which starts the magnetization at $-M_0$ instead.  We take that up in the inversion recovery chapter (@fig-ch10-inversion-recovery-spin-lattice-t1-1), where the negative starting value is the point of the measurement rather than a complication.

::: {.callout-note title="T1 relaxation"}
### Typical $T_1$ Relaxation Times (in seconds)

| Tissue | At 1.5 Tesla | At 3.0 Tesla |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Gray Matter (GM) | ~0.88 s (range: 0.85 – 0.95 s) | ~1.20 s - 1.35 s |
| White Matter (WM) | ~0.65 s (range: 0.60 – 0.75 s) | ~0.83 s - 0.86 s |
| CSF | ~4.0 s | ~4.3 s |
:::

Try plugging the different $T_1$ relaxation times for gray matter, white matter, and CSF into the slider below to see how each tissue's longitudinal magnetization curve behaves and recovers over time.   

{{< include includes/ch07-fig-t1-recover.qmd >}}

As you will see, there is not a huge difference in the recovery rate between gray and white matter.  But it is enough so that we can create an image where the two types of brain differ. 


## Longitudinal relaxation rates

![Longitudinal relaxation rate depends on your neighborhood: recovery curves for gray matter (T1 = 0.88 s) and white matter (T1 = 0.65 s) at 1.5 T.](images/ch07/longitudinal-relaxation-rate-depends-on-your-neigh.png){#fig-ch07-longitudinal-relaxation-rate-depends-on-your-neigh}

The recovery depends on the environment around the spins—for example, gray matter versus white matter. One second after the pulse, gray matter has recovered less longitudinal magnetization than white matter because its $T_1$ is longer. This difference in recovery, which reflects tissue chemistry and structure, gives us contrast between CSF, gray matter, and white matter.

Within the brain, the differences are small but measurable. At 1.5 T, the $T_1$ of gray matter is about 0.88 s and the $T_1$ of white matter about 0.65 s. In this simplified comparison, with the same equilibrium magnetization, white matter recovers faster and produces the larger signal during recovery.

## Contrast: the difference between signals

![Contrast: the difference between signals: the gray/white magnetization difference is largest around 0.8 s after the RF pulse.](images/ch07/contrast-the-difference-between-signals.png){#fig-ch07-contrast-the-difference-between-signals}

An image does not show signal level alone. Nearby tissues are distinguished largely by the *difference* between their signals—the image contrast.

The two normalized recovery curves in @fig-ch07-longitudinal-relaxation-rate-depends-on-your-neigh start together at zero and end together at $M_0$. In this equal-$M_0$ simulation, the difference is therefore zero at both ends and largest somewhere in between. @fig-ch07-contrast-the-difference-between-signals plots that difference,

$$
\Delta M = M_0\left(e^{-t/T_{1,G}} - e^{-t/T_{1,W}}\right)
$$

Here, $G$ and $W$ denote gray and white matter.

The contrast for this particular simulation peaks around 0.8 s after the RF pulse at 1.5 T. This is a useful result: it tells us when to read out the signal in this simple experiment. Waiting too long is as bad as not waiting long enough, because both tissues have then nearly recovered to the same value. Choosing acquisition timing to emphasize a contrast of interest is a central design problem for a pulse sequence.

## The T1-contrast distinguishes gray and white matter

![The T1-contrast distinguishes gray and white matter.](images/ch07/the-t1-contrast-distinguishes-gray-and-white-matte.png){#fig-ch07-the-t1-contrast-distinguishes-gray-and-white-matte}

Putting the two ideas together: a longer $T_1$ means slower recovery and therefore a smaller signal at readout, when the other factors are held fixed. In this example, white matter (short $T_1$) is bright, gray matter is darker, and CSF (longest $T_1$ of the three) is darkest. This is the appearance of the images here, and it is why $T_1$-weighted volumes are widely used to separate gray matter from white matter and to measure cortical thickness, atrophy, or ventricular enlargement.

## Surface Interaction Rate (SIR)

![Surface Interaction Rate (SIR); portraits of Bloch and Purcell (Huettel et al., *Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging*, 2e, Fig. 1.13).](images/ch07/surface-interaction-rate-sir.png){#fig-ch07-surface-interaction-rate-sir}

The $T_1$ of free water is long because there are no nearby large molecules to absorb the excess energy efficiently. Freely moving water molecules have relatively few effective ways to pass that energy to their surroundings. Near a membrane or other macromolecule, the interaction is stronger, so the energy transfer is more efficient and $T_1$ becomes shorter. BPP theory explains why the $T_1$ of bulk free water is about 4.3 s at room temperature and is approximately independent of $B_0$ over the usual MRI field range [@bloembergen1948-relaxation]. Yes, you should be amazed.

The $T_1$ values for brain tissue, which contains many large molecules and membranes, are much shorter than the value for free water (0.65–0.9 s for white and gray matter at 1.5 T). Much of the water in tissue is near a macromolecular surface. Interactions between the water and those large molecules speed up the transfer of energy to the surrounding environment, shortening $T_1$. As a rough approximation, the $T_1$ we measure in a voxel tells us how efficiently water in the hydration layer exchanges energy with nearby molecules.
